title: Database isolation and consistency: CAP, isolation levels, and locking
description: CAP, isolation levels, and locking, as the docs and papers define them. Learn why partition tolerance is never optional, what PostgreSQL's default Read Committed lets through, why snapshot isolation allows write skew, how linearizability differs from serializability, and when to use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, an advisory lock, or a version column.

questions.title: In Gilbert and Lynch's formulation of CAP, why can't you just choose not to tolerate partitions?
questions.description: CAP is usually taught as "consistency, availability, partition tolerance: pick two." People often call single-node PostgreSQL "a CA system."

options.text: A partition is a network failure that happens to you, not a property you pick. You only get to choose how the system behaves when one happens.
The SQL standard requires partition tolerance from any system that claims ACID transactions.
Giving up partition tolerance would also mean giving up durability, and no database will do that.
Modern datacenter networks no longer partition, so P comes for free and can be ignored.

questions.explanation:
"Pick two of three" makes CA sound like a real option. It isn't one.

Gilbert and Lynch's theorem assumes an asynchronous network that can lose messages, and the proof is a partition argument. Split the nodes into two halves that can't talk to each other. Write on one side and read on the other. If both sides answer, as availability requires, the reader gets a stale value, so the system isn't linearizable.

The network decides when a partition happens. The system only decides how to respond. A "CA" database is one that hasn't said what it does when the network breaks. In practice it stops serving requests, which is CP behavior. Brewer made the same point in his retrospective twelve years later: the useful question is what you give up during a partition and how you recover afterwards.

CAP's three letters are also narrower than they sound. C means linearizability, not ACID consistency or snapshot isolation. A means every request to every non-failed node gets a non-error response. That bar is so high that a single-leader system fails it even when the network is healthy. Kleppmann argues that under these definitions most real systems are neither CP nor AP.

- [Eric Brewer: CAP Twelve Years Later: How the "Rules" Have Changed (IEEE Computer, 2012)](https://www.infoq.com/articles/cap-twelve-years-later-how-the-rules-have-changed/)

questions.title: Does the C in CAP mean the same thing as the C in ACID?

options.text: No. CAP's C is linearizability, a guarantee about how fresh your reads are. ACID's C means your application's invariants hold, and the database only enforces the ones you declare as constraints.
Yes. Both mean that a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another valid state.
Yes. Both are serializability, described from a distributed and a single-node perspective.
No. CAP's C means durability of committed writes, while ACID's C means isolation between concurrent transactions.

questions.explanation:
The shared letter is an accident of history. ACID was picked because it spells a word, and C is its weakest member.

ACID consistency says a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another. "Valid" means your invariants: foreign keys, `CHECK` constraints, "this balance never goes negative." The database enforces the constraints you declared and leaves the rest to you. Nothing about it is distributed.

CAP's C is linearizability, a recency guarantee on single objects. Every read sees the latest completed write, as if there were only one copy of the data. It says nothing about invariants that span several objects.

In *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, Kleppmann says the C in ACID doesn't really belong in the acronym, and that CAP reusing the letter for an unrelated property has muddled architecture arguments for years.

- [Kleppmann: Please stop calling databases CP or AP](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2015/05/11/please-stop-calling-databases-cp-or-ap.html)

questions.title: What does the ELC half of Abadi's PACELC add to the picture that CAP leaves out?
questions.description: CAP only describes what happens during a partition. Daniel Abadi's 2012 extension covers the normal case.

options.text: That when the network is healthy, a replicated system still trades latency against consistency, because staying consistent costs round trips.
That when the network is healthy, a system must choose between elasticity and cost, the two economic axes of cloud deployment.
That outside of transactions, a system trades encryption against latency when replicating across regions.
That when a node is overloaded, a system chooses between shedding load and queueing it, which CAP treats as a partition.

questions.explanation:
PACELC reads: if there's a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.

Abadi's point is that CAP covers a rare case and ignores the 99.99% of the time when the network is fine. The tradeoff doesn't go away then. To keep replicas linearizable, you have to coordinate with them before you acknowledge a write, and that costs a round trip on every request. A quorum write across regions costs tens or hundreds of milliseconds whether or not anything is broken.

This makes PACELC's labels more informative than CAP's. DynamoDB and Cassandra are PA/EL: they give up consistency during partitions and for lower latency. VoltDB and Spanner-style systems are PC/EC and always pay the coordination cost. MongoDB is usually described as PA/EC. The question changes from "which two do we pick?" to "what is a round trip worth to us?"

questions.title: How do linearizability and serializability differ as correctness properties?

options.text: Linearizability is a real-time recency guarantee on single operations over single objects. Serializability says a set of multi-object transactions is equivalent to some serial order, with no real-time requirement.
They are the same property. "Linearizability" is the distributed-systems name and "serializability" is the database name.
Linearizability applies to transactions and serializability applies to individual reads and writes, the opposite of how the terms sound.
Linearizability is strictly weaker than serializability: every linearizable system is serializable, but not the reverse.

questions.explanation:
They are guarantees on two different axes, so neither implies the other.

Linearizability (Herlihy and Wing, 1990) covers single operations on single objects, and it cares about wall-clock time. If operation A finishes before operation B starts, everyone must see A before B. A replicated register behaves as if there were exactly one copy.

Serializability (Papadimitriou, 1979) covers multi-object transactions. It only says the result equals some serial execution, and any order will do. A serializable database may order a transaction that ran at 10:00 after one that ran at 11:00.

This has concrete effects. A serializable but non-linearizable system can give you a stale snapshot: your write commits, a later read-only transaction is ordered before it, and it correctly doesn't see your write. A linearizable but non-serializable store, such as a single-node key-value store with atomic per-key operations, gives perfect recency per key and no protection against write skew across two keys.

Bailis sums it up: linearizability is about time, serializability is about transaction order. Having both is called strict serializability.

- [Peter Bailis: Linearizability versus Serializability](http://www.bailis.org/blog/linearizability-versus-serializability/)
- [Herlihy & Wing: Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects (TOPLAS, 1990)](https://cs.brown.edu/~mph/HerlihyW90/p463-herlihy.pdf)
- [Jepsen: Consistency Models](https://jepsen.io/consistency)

questions.title: When a distributed database's marketing promises "strong consistency," which formal property does it almost always mean?

options.text: Linearizability. Reads observe the latest committed write in real time, as if there were a single copy of each object.
Serializability. Concurrent transactions are equivalent to some serial execution.
The C in ACID. Declared constraints such as foreign keys and `CHECK` are never violated.
Durability. An acknowledged write survives the loss of any single node.

questions.explanation:
"Strong consistency" has no formal definition in the literature. Vendors use it as shorthand for linearizability, and the Spanner and DynamoDB docs both use the phrase that way. It's a claim about recency: you won't read a stale value from a replica.

That leaves a lot open. A store can be linearizable per key and still let two transactions read a shared invariant and both break it, because linearizability says nothing about multi-object transactions. DynamoDB's `ConsistentRead` is exactly this: strongly consistent per item, with no transactional isolation.

Jepsen's consistency map helps here. It draws linearizability and serializability as separate properties that meet only at strict serializability. When a vendor says "strongly consistent," ask whether they mean per object or across transactions.

- [AWS: DynamoDB read consistency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.ReadConsistency.html)
- [Peter Bailis: Linearizability versus Serializability](http://www.bailis.org/blog/linearizability-versus-serializability/)

questions.title: What does strict serializability guarantee that plain serializability does not?

options.text: That the equivalent serial order also respects real time, so a transaction that committed before another began is ordered before it.
That transactions never abort, because the system picks the serial order in advance.
That every transaction executes literally one at a time, with no concurrency in the implementation.
That reads never block writes, which plain serializability achieves only under two-phase locking.

questions.explanation:
Strict serializability is serializability plus linearizability. Serializability only says some serial order exists. Strict serializability ties that order to wall-clock time.

The difference shows up as the "my write vanished" bug. Plain serializability allows this: T1 writes `x = 1` and commits at 10:00:00. Then read-only T2 starts at 10:00:05 and returns `x = 0`. The system says the serial order was T2, then T1. That's fully serializable, and useless to a user who just saw their save succeed.

Strict serializability forbids it. That's why Spanner (via TrueTime) and FoundationDB advertise it, and it's what most people assume "serializable" means. Single-node PostgreSQL at `SERIALIZABLE` is effectively strict for committed transactions, because there's one commit order and one clock. Route reads to a replica and you lose the strictness, even though every transaction is still serializable.

- [Jepsen: Strict Serializability](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/strict-serializable)
- [Google: Spanner, TrueTime and the CAP Theorem](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//pubs/archive/45855.pdf)

questions.title: Herlihy and Wing proved that linearizability is local (composable). What does that give you, and does serializability have it too?

options.text: Compose linearizable objects and the whole system is linearizable, so each object can be implemented independently. Serializability is not local: two individually serializable stores combined are not serializable.
Both properties compose, which is why sharding a serializable database across independent nodes preserves serializability for free.
Neither composes. Both require a global coordinator, which is why every linearizable system has a single leader.
Locality means linearizable objects must live on the same machine, so it argues against distributing them.

questions.explanation:
Locality is why linearizability shows up everywhere in distributed-systems design. Herlihy and Wing's theorem says a system is linearizable if and only if each of its objects is. Build a linearizable register, queue, and counter separately, put them together, and the whole is linearizable without re-checking anything.

Serializability doesn't compose, and the counterexample is small. Take two stores, X and Y, each serializable on its own, and two transactions:

```text
T1: write X=1, read Y   -> sees Y=0
T2: write Y=1, read X   -> sees X=0
```

Store X can order T1 before T2. Store Y can order T2 before T1. Each store is serializable alone. Together there's no serial order, because each transaction would have to come before the other. That's why sharding a database doesn't give you global serializability for free. You need cross-shard machinery, such as two-phase commit, a global sequencer, or distributed SSI.

So each property has a limit. Linearizability composes but covers only one object. Serializability spans objects but doesn't compose.

- [Jepsen: Consistency Models](https://jepsen.io/consistency)

questions.title: A read-only transaction at `SERIALIZABLE` returns data you know is out of date. Has the database violated serializability?

options.text: Not necessarily. Serializability requires only that some equivalent serial order exists, and the system may place your read-only transaction early in that order.
Yes. `SERIALIZABLE` is the strongest level defined by the SQL standard, so a stale read is by definition a bug.
Yes, but only for read-only transactions. Read-write transactions may observe stale snapshots.
No, because `SERIALIZABLE` promises snapshot isolation rather than any real-time guarantee.

questions.explanation:
Serializability promises equivalence to some serial order. It says nothing about freshness, and that serial order doesn't have to agree with the clock.

A database that ordered every read-only transaction before every write would be trivially serializable and useless. Real systems don't go that far, but they do use this freedom in ways you'll meet in production.

A hot standby serving `SERIALIZABLE` reads lags the primary by the replication delay. Every transaction is still serializable. The serial order just trails real time.

PostgreSQL's `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` goes further. It waits for a snapshot it can prove is free of anomalies, then reads it without predicate-lock tracking and with no risk of aborting. The docs note this is the only case where a serializable transaction blocks and a repeatable read one doesn't. You give up freshness for a read that never needs a retry.

If the read must reflect real time, you need strict serializability, or linearizability on that object. In practice that usually means reading from the primary.

- [PostgreSQL: SET TRANSACTION, READ ONLY DEFERRABLE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-set-transaction.html)
- [Peter Bailis: Linearizability versus Serializability](http://www.bailis.org/blog/linearizability-versus-serializability/)

questions.title: Bailis et al. asked which isolation levels a system can provide while remaining available during a partition. Which of these made the cut?
questions.description: A *Highly Available Transaction* (HAT) system is one whose replicas answer every request without coordinating, so it stays up under any partition.

options.text: Read Committed.
Snapshot Isolation.
Repeatable Read.
One-copy serializability.

questions.explanation:
The *Highly Available Transactions* paper draws the line clearly. In a HAT system, every replica answers every request without contacting anyone else, so it never blocks, even when fully partitioned. That splits the isolation levels into two groups.

Achievable: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Monotonic Atomic View, item and predicate cut isolation, and the session guarantees (monotonic reads, monotonic writes, and read-your-writes, which needs sticky routing).

Not achievable: Cursor Stability, Snapshot Isolation, Repeatable Read, one-copy serializability, and anything linearizable.

The unavailable levels all fail for the same reason. They must prevent a conflicting transaction somewhere else, and detecting one takes communication that a partition blocks. Snapshot Isolation is the interesting case: first-committer-wins has to detect write-write conflicts, and that check is itself coordination.

Read Committed being achievable is a big reason it's the default in so many systems. It's also why "let's just turn on Serializable everywhere" costs far more in a geo-replicated deployment than on one machine.
questions.references:
- [Bailis, Davidson, Fekete, Ghodsi, Hellerstein, Stoica: Highly Available Transactions: Virtues and Limitations (VLDB 2014)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol7/p181-bailis.pdf)
- [Bailis et al.: Coordination Avoidance in Database Systems (VLDB 2015)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p185-bailis.pdf)

questions.title: What is the strongest consistency model a system can offer if it must stay available under any partition and still converge?

options.text: Causal consistency. Operations related by happens-before are seen in that order by everyone, while concurrent operations may be seen in different orders.
Sequential consistency. Everyone observes the same total order of operations, just not necessarily the real-time one.
Snapshot isolation. Every transaction reads a consistent snapshot, with write-write conflicts rejected.
Eventual consistency. Anything stronger, including causal consistency, requires coordination.

questions.explanation:
This result is more useful than CAP because it names the ceiling instead of only proving something impossible. Mahajan, Alvisi, and Dahlin showed that real-time causal consistency is the strongest model an always-available, one-way convergent system can offer. Attiya, Ellen, and Morrison later refined this for eventually consistent stores, showing that observable causal consistency is optimal for a natural class of data types.

The line falls there because causal consistency only needs you to track and respect happens-before, and that's metadata that travels with the writes. A partitioned replica can keep accepting writes, tag each one with its causal dependencies, and reconcile later. Sequential consistency needs everyone to agree on one total order, and agreeing on anything across a partition takes coordination you don't have.

This is the theory behind causal+ systems such as COPS, Antidote, and MongoDB's causally consistent sessions, and behind CRDTs. They offer the strongest model that's still always available, instead of settling for plain eventual consistency.

- [Mahajan, Alvisi, Dahlin: Consistency, Availability, and Convergence (UTCS TR-11-22)](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/lorenzo/papers/cac-tr.pdf)
- [Attiya, Ellen, Morrison: Limitations of Highly-Available Eventually-Consistent Data Stores (PODC 2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02275)
- [Jepsen: Causal Consistency](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/causal)

questions.title: Which transaction isolation level does a stock PostgreSQL server use when you `BEGIN` without specifying one?
questions.description: Answer with the level's name, for example `read uncommitted`.

images.alt: Four PostgreSQL isolation level names against what the server actually does. READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted for compatibility and treated as READ COMMITTED. READ COMMITTED, the default, takes a fresh snapshot at the start of every statement rather than of the transaction. REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation: one snapshot per transaction, ruling out dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms while letting write skew and lost update through. SERIALIZABLE adds SSI, which watches for dangerous read/write structures and aborts a transaction instead of taking two-phase locks. Two cards give the SQLSTATE codes to retry on, 40001 serialization_failure and 40P01 deadlock_detected, and a closing note warns that SSI only sees transactions that are themselves SERIALIZABLE, that Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, and that MySQL's InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ.
images.caption: The highlighted row is what a bare `BEGIN` gives you.

questions.explanation:
PostgreSQL ships with `default_transaction_isolation = 'read committed'`, and most production databases never change it. Every ORM connection, every `BEGIN` in a migration, and every `psql` session starts there unless you ask for something else.

This matters more than it seems. Common beliefs like "the database handles concurrency" or "transactions are isolated" assume serializability. Read Committed allows non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates in read-modify-write code, and write skew. Its only promise about other transactions is that you'll never see their uncommitted data.

You can check and change it per session or globally:

```sql
SHOW default_transaction_isolation;   -- read committed

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- ...
COMMIT;
```

Raising the default to `repeatable read` or `serializable` is a reasonable choice, but it affects application code. Transactions can now fail with SQLSTATE `40001` at any statement, so add a retry loop to every transaction before you switch.

- [PostgreSQL: Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
- [PostgreSQL: default_transaction_isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html#GUC-DEFAULT-TRANSACTION-ISOLATION)

questions.title: PostgreSQL accepts all four SQL-standard isolation level names. How many levels with distinct behavior does it actually implement?

images.alt: Four PostgreSQL isolation level names against what the server actually does. READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted for compatibility and treated as READ COMMITTED. READ COMMITTED, the default, takes a fresh snapshot at the start of every statement rather than of the transaction. REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation: one snapshot per transaction, ruling out dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms while letting write skew and lost update through. SERIALIZABLE adds SSI, which watches for dangerous read/write structures and aborts a transaction instead of taking two-phase locks. Two cards give the SQLSTATE codes to retry on, 40001 serialization_failure and 40P01 deadlock_detected, and a closing note warns that SSI only sees transactions that are themselves SERIALIZABLE, that Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, and that MySQL's InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ.
images.caption: Four rows, but the first is an alias for the second.

questions.explanation:
Three: Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable. PostgreSQL accepts `READ UNCOMMITTED` for standards compatibility and treats it as Read Committed.

The reason is architectural. PostgreSQL's MVCC never shows an uncommitted row version to another transaction. A tuple becomes visible only after the transaction that inserted it commits. No code path could show you a dirty row, so dirty reads can't happen at all, and the weakest standard level maps onto the next one up.

The standard allows this. It defines each level by the anomalies it must prevent, so an implementation may be stricter. PostgreSQL does this twice: its Repeatable Read is also stricter than required, because it's full snapshot isolation and prevents phantom reads too.

```sql
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED;
SHOW transaction_isolation;   -- read uncommitted (the name is remembered)
-- ...but no dirty read can ever occur
```
questions.references: - [PostgreSQL: Transaction Isolation, table of levels and anomalies](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

questions.title: At `READ COMMITTED`, when does PostgreSQL take the snapshot a query sees?

images.alt: Four PostgreSQL isolation level names against what the server actually does. READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted for compatibility and treated as READ COMMITTED. READ COMMITTED, the default, takes a fresh snapshot at the start of every statement rather than of the transaction. REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation: one snapshot per transaction, ruling out dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms while letting write skew and lost update through. SERIALIZABLE adds SSI, which watches for dangerous read/write structures and aborts a transaction instead of taking two-phase locks. Two cards give the SQLSTATE codes to retry on, 40001 serialization_failure and 40P01 deadlock_detected, and a closing note warns that SSI only sees transactions that are themselves SERIALIZABLE, that Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, and that MySQL's InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ.
images.caption: Per statement, not per transaction.

options.text: At the start of each individual statement, so two identical `SELECT`s in one transaction can legitimately return different rows.
At `BEGIN`, so every statement in the transaction sees the same consistent snapshot.
At the first statement that acquires a row lock. Statements before it read the live state directly.
At `COMMIT` time, retroactively, which is how PostgreSQL detects conflicts without locking readers.

questions.explanation:
One sentence in the PostgreSQL docs explains most Read Committed surprises: a `SELECT` query sees "a snapshot of the database as of the instant the query begins to run." Each statement gets its own snapshot.

So this is correct behavior at Read Committed, and it's the non-repeatable read anomaly:

```sql
BEGIN;                                   -- isolation level: read committed
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;   -- 100

--    meanwhile, another session:
--    UPDATE accounts SET balance = 50 WHERE id = 1; COMMIT;

SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;   -- 50   (!)
COMMIT;
```

In application code, this means any invariant you check in one query and act on in another is unprotected. Any committed change can land between the two statements. A report built from several `SELECT`s can contradict itself, because the totals query and the detail query may see different data.

`REPEATABLE READ` takes one snapshot at the transaction's first statement and keeps it until the transaction ends.

questions.title: What does the concurrent `DELETE` do, and why?

options.text: Nothing at all. It skips the row that was 9, because its snapshot saw 9 rather than 10, and by the time it locks the row that was 10, that row has become 11 and no longer matches.
It deletes exactly one row, the one whose value was 10 when the `DELETE` began, because Read Committed uses the statement's original snapshot throughout.
It deletes both rows, because after the `UPDATE` commits the re-check sees values 10 and 11 and re-evaluates the predicate against the whole table.
It fails with a serialization error, because the rows it selected were concurrently modified.

questions.explanation:
This example comes from the PostgreSQL docs. It's worth knowing because Read Committed produces a result here that matches no snapshot at all.

Look at the two rows separately.

The row with `hits = 9`: the `DELETE`'s snapshot sees 9, which doesn't match `hits = 10`, so the `DELETE` never considers it. It can't see that the `UPDATE` is about to make it 10.

The row with `hits = 10`: the snapshot matches, so the `DELETE` tries to lock the row and waits, because the `UPDATE` holds it. When the `UPDATE` commits, Read Committed re-checks the condition against the new version (the source code calls this step EvalPlanQual). The value is now 11, so the row no longer matches and is skipped.

Nothing is deleted, even though a row with `hits = 10` existed both before and after the `UPDATE`. The docs sum it up: "it is possible for an updating command to see an inconsistent snapshot: it can see the effects of concurrent updating commands on the same rows it is trying to update, but it does not see effects of those commands on other rows in the database." Read Committed works well for `WHERE id = ?` point updates and is unreliable for complex search conditions.
questions.references: - [PostgreSQL: Read Committed Isolation Level, the `website`/`hits` example](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-READ-COMMITTED)

questions.title: Two sessions concurrently run `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1` at `READ COMMITTED`. Is one of the deductions lost?

options.text: No. The second `UPDATE` blocks on the row lock, then re-reads the newly committed version and subtracts from that, so both deductions apply.
Yes. Both statements read `balance` from their own snapshot, so the second write overwrites the first and one deduction disappears.
No. PostgreSQL detects the write-write conflict and aborts the second transaction with SQLSTATE `40001`.
It depends on timing. If the statements overlap, one deduction is lost; if they don't, both apply.

questions.explanation:
Read Committed handles this case well, and seeing why makes the next few failures easier to understand.

When the second `UPDATE` reaches a row that another uncommitted transaction has changed, it waits on the row lock. When the first transaction commits, the second one doesn't continue with its old snapshot. It re-reads the latest committed version of the row, re-checks the `WHERE` clause, and re-evaluates the `SET` expression. So `balance - 100` uses the balance after the first update. Start at 500 and you always end at 300.

The docs call this out as the reason Read Committed is "just right for simpler cases": "Because each command is affecting only a predetermined row, letting it see the updated version of the row does not create any troublesome inconsistency."

This only works *inside a single statement*. If you split the logic into two statements (read the balance into the application, compute there, and write the result back), none of this protection applies, and you do lose updates. The safety comes from doing the arithmetic inside the `UPDATE`, not from the isolation level.
questions.references: - [PostgreSQL: Read Committed Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-READ-COMMITTED)

questions.title: Both transactions commit successfully. What is the final `balance`, and what is this anomaly called?

images.alt: Three two-transaction timelines with time running downward, all of them committing. Lost update at READ COMMITTED: both sessions read balance 100, one writes 90 and commits, the other writes 80 and commits, leaving 80 and erasing the first change. Write skew at REPEATABLE READ: two doctors each count two colleagues on call, each concludes it is safe to leave, each updates a different row, and both commit with nobody on call. The phantom a row lock cannot hold, at READ COMMITTED: two sessions run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, both get zero rows, both insert a booking for the same room and hour, and both commit.
images.caption: The first timeline: two reads of 100, two writes, one survivor.

options.text: `80`. T1's deduction is silently overwritten. This is a lost update, and Read Committed does not prevent it.
`70`. Both deductions apply, because the second `UPDATE` re-reads the committed row before writing.
`80`, but the anomaly is a write skew, since two transactions read the same value and wrote conflicting results.
T2 aborts with a serialization failure, so the final balance is `90`.

questions.explanation:
T1 writes 90 and commits. T2 still holds the 100 it read before T1 committed, so it writes 80. Both succeed, and T1's change is gone. The database followed its rules. Read Committed just doesn't guard against this pattern.

Compare `SET balance = balance - 100`. There, the read and write are one statement, so the re-check after the lock wait recomputes the arithmetic. Here, the read was a separate statement, the value went into application memory, and the later `UPDATE` writes a fixed number. `SET balance = 80` gives the database no hint that it depends on an earlier read, so it can't detect the conflict.

Lost update isn't one of ANSI SQL-92's named anomalies. Berenson et al. added it as P4 in their 1995 critique because the standard's list missed real, common failures. Four ways to fix it:

1. Do the arithmetic in SQL: `SET balance = balance - 10`.
2. Use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` to lock the row before reading it.
3. Add an optimistic version column: `WHERE id = 1 AND version = 7`.
4. Raise the level to `REPEATABLE READ`, where T2's `UPDATE` fails with SQLSTATE `40001`.

questions.title: Which of these anomalies does PostgreSQL's `REPEATABLE READ` prevent?
questions.description: Select every anomaly that this level rules out, as PostgreSQL implements it.

options.text: Dirty reads.
Non-repeatable reads.
Phantom reads.
Lost updates, by silently serializing the conflicting writes.
Write skew.

questions.explanation:
PostgreSQL's `REPEATABLE READ` is snapshot isolation, which is stricter than the SQL standard's Repeatable Read. The transaction takes one snapshot at its first statement and reads from it until it ends, so dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads can't happen. The standard allows phantoms at this level, but a snapshot can't gain new rows.

Snapshot isolation doesn't prevent write skew. Two transactions read an overlapping set of rows, check an invariant, and write to different rows. There's no write-write conflict, both commit, and the invariant breaks. This gap led to Fekete et al.'s work and, later, to PostgreSQL's SSI.

Lost updates are the tricky option. Snapshot isolation does stop the read-modify-write lost update, but it does so by aborting the second transaction's `UPDATE`:

```text
ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
```

That's SQLSTATE `40001`, and your application has to catch it and retry the whole transaction. An error you must handle is a different contract from silent prevention, which is why the option as written is wrong. If you raise the isolation level without adding retries, you swap a silent data-corruption bug for a visible availability bug.

questions.explanation:
SQLSTATE `40001`, `serialization_failure`. It's the most important error to handle in any application running above Read Committed. The message depends on what detected the conflict:

```text
ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
HINT:   The transaction might succeed if retried.
```

The first comes from Repeatable Read or Serializable hitting a write-write conflict. The second means SSI found a dangerous pattern of read-write dependencies. Both mean the same thing in practice: your data is fine, so retry the whole transaction from `BEGIN`.

Two things catch people out. First, retrying only the failed statement is wrong. The transaction's snapshot is already invalid, so you must replay from the start, and your application needs to be able to re-run the whole unit of work. Second, `40001` has a sibling, `40P01` (`deadlock_detected`). Both are in class 40, transaction rollback, and both are safe to retry. A good retry helper usually catches the whole class, with exponential backoff to avoid livelock.

options.text: A deadlock was detected and PostgreSQL broke the cycle by killing your transaction. Retry the whole transaction, and ideally make lock acquisition order consistent.
SSI detected a serialization anomaly. Retrying is pointless until the conflicting transaction finishes, so the client should back off for at least a second.
The connection was lost mid-transaction, so the client must reconnect before it can retry.
A lock wait exceeded `lock_timeout`. Raise the timeout, since retrying will hit the same wait.

questions.explanation:
`40P01` is `deadlock_detected`. After a transaction has waited for `deadlock_timeout` (1s by default), PostgreSQL runs its deadlock detector. If it finds a cycle in the wait-for graph, it aborts one transaction to break it:

```text
ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL: Process 4711 waits for ShareLock on transaction 1234; blocked by process 4712.
        Process 4712 waits for ShareLock on transaction 1235; blocked by process 4711.
```

Retrying is correct and usually succeeds, because the other transaction has finished by then. Unlike `40001`, though, a deadlock often points to a design problem you can fix. The usual cause is two code paths locking the same rows in opposite orders: one updates account 1 then 2, the other 2 then 1. Lock rows in a consistent order, with `ORDER BY id` in the `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or by always touching ids in ascending order, and the cycle can't form.

Deadlocks don't depend on the isolation level. They happen at Read Committed too, wherever explicit or implicit row locks are taken. `40001` and `40P01` are both in SQLSTATE class 40 and belong in the same retry handler. The difference is that a rising `40P01` rate tells you to fix your lock ordering.

questions.title: Both transactions commit and nobody is left on call. Why did snapshot isolation allow it?
questions.description:
Alice and Bob are both on call. The rule is that at least one doctor must stay on call. Both feel unwell and try to go off call at the same time, at `REPEATABLE READ` (snapshot isolation):

```sql
-- Alice                                    -- Bob
BEGIN;                                      BEGIN;
SELECT count(*) FROM doctors                SELECT count(*) FROM doctors
 WHERE on_call = true                        WHERE on_call = true
   AND shift_id = 1234;   -- 2                  AND shift_id = 1234;   -- 2
-- 2 >= 2, safe to leave                    -- 2 >= 2, safe to leave
UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false          UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false
 WHERE name = 'Alice'                        WHERE name = 'Bob'
   AND shift_id = 1234;                        AND shift_id = 1234;
COMMIT;                                     COMMIT;
```

images.alt: Three two-transaction timelines with time running downward, all of them committing. Lost update at READ COMMITTED: both sessions read balance 100, one writes 90 and commits, the other writes 80 and commits, leaving 80 and erasing the first change. Write skew at REPEATABLE READ: two doctors each count two colleagues on call, each concludes it is safe to leave, each updates a different row, and both commit with nobody on call. The phantom a row lock cannot hold, at READ COMMITTED: two sessions run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, both get zero rows, both insert a booking for the same room and hour, and both commit.
images.caption: The second timeline: different rows, so no write-write conflict to detect.

options.text: Because the two transactions wrote different rows, so first-committer-wins had no write-write conflict to detect, yet each write broke the premise the other had read.
Because the `SELECT count(*)` ran before the snapshot was taken, so both transactions read pre-transaction data.
Because `count(*)` is an aggregate, and PostgreSQL does not track aggregates for conflict detection at any isolation level.
Because snapshot isolation only checks invariants declared as `CHECK` constraints, and this one was enforced in application code.

questions.explanation:
This is write skew, which Berenson et al. catalogued as anomaly A5B. It's the main gap in snapshot isolation.

It always has the same shape. Two transactions read an overlapping set of rows, each makes a decision based on what it read, and each writes a row the other didn't write. Snapshot isolation's only conflict check is first-committer-wins, which fires when two concurrent transactions change the same row. Alice changed her row and Bob changed his, so both commit.

It's hard to catch in code review because neither transaction is wrong on its own. Each read a valid state, applied a valid rule, and wrote a valid row. The invariant, "at least one doctor on call," spans several rows, and snapshot isolation doesn't know about it. The underlying problem is a read-write dependency: Alice's write invalidated something Bob had read, and Bob's write did the same to Alice. With two such edges forming a cycle, no serial order exists.

Once you know the shape, you'll see it often: double-spending against a balance check, two users claiming the last seat, a uniqueness rule enforced by `SELECT` before `INSERT`, double-booked meeting rooms. To fix it, use `SERIALIZABLE`, which detects exactly this; put the conflict on a shared row you lock; or add a real constraint the database enforces itself, such as `EXCLUDE` or a unique index.

images.alt: Three two-transaction timelines with time running downward, all of them committing. Lost update at READ COMMITTED: both sessions read balance 100, one writes 90 and commits, the other writes 80 and commits, leaving 80 and erasing the first change. images.caption: It compares writes, and write skew never writes the same row twice.

options.text: Read-write conflicts, where one transaction writes a row that another transaction read and based a decision on.
Write-write conflicts on the same row, which is why lost updates survive at snapshot isolation.
Conflicts involving rows inserted after the snapshot was taken, which are visible only to `SERIALIZABLE`.
Conflicts between transactions that started at different times, since the rule compares only concurrent snapshots.

questions.explanation:
First-committer-wins detects write-write conflicts and nothing else. When two concurrent transactions change the same row, the second to commit is rejected. PostgreSQL uses the equivalent first-updater-wins variant with row locks, so the loser usually finds out at `UPDATE` rather than at `COMMIT`. That's enough to prevent dirty writes and read-modify-write lost updates.

It can't see a read-write dependency (also called an rw-antidependency), where T2 writes a row that T1 read, so T1's view is now out of date. That pattern never involves two writes to one row. In a pure MVCC snapshot scheme, reads leave no trace at all: they take no locks and change no tuples, so nothing records that T1 ever looked.

That's why serializability needs something extra. PostgreSQL's SSI adds SIREAD locks, which exist only to record what each transaction read, so rw edges become visible and cycles can be found. The rest of SSI's design follows from this blind spot.

questions.title: PostgreSQL's Serializable Snapshot Isolation aborts a transaction when it spots a "dangerous structure." What is that structure?
questions.description: SSI arrived in PostgreSQL 9.1. It's what makes `SERIALIZABLE` truly serializable instead of snapshot isolation under a stronger name.

images.alt: Four PostgreSQL isolation level names against what the server actually does. READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted for compatibility and treated as READ COMMITTED. READ COMMITTED, the default, takes a fresh snapshot at the start of every statement rather than of the transaction. REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation: one snapshot per transaction, ruling out dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms while letting write skew and lost update through. SERIALIZABLE adds SSI, which watches for dangerous read/write structures and aborts a transaction instead of taking two-phase locks. Two cards give the SQLSTATE codes to retry on, 40001 serialization_failure and 40P01 deadlock_detected, and a closing note warns that SSI only sees transactions that are themselves SERIALIZABLE, that Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, and that MySQL's InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ.
images.caption: The fourth row: SSI watches for the structure, then aborts.

options.text: A transaction with both an incoming and an outgoing read-write dependency, called a pivot. Under snapshot isolation, every cycle in the dependency graph must contain two such consecutive edges.
Any cycle at all in the wait-for graph, which is the same condition the deadlock detector uses.
Two transactions that have written to the same row within the same snapshot window.
A transaction that has held predicate locks for longer than `deadlock_timeout` without committing.

questions.explanation:
SSI works in practice thanks to a theorem by Fekete et al.: under snapshot isolation, every cycle in the serialization dependency graph contains at least two consecutive rw-antidependency edges. So you never have to build the whole graph and search it for cycles. You only watch for one local pattern:

```text
     rw            rw
Tin ----> Tpivot ----> Tout
```

A transaction with an incoming rw edge and an outgoing rw edge is a pivot, and every cycle needs one. PostgreSQL tracks these edges with SIREAD locks: lightweight, non-blocking markers that record what each transaction read, at tuple, page, or relation granularity. It aborts a transaction when the pattern completes, with one refinement: `Tout` must commit first for a real cycle to exist.

This has two consequences. Because a pivot is necessary but not sufficient for a cycle, SSI has false positives and will sometimes abort a transaction that would have been fine. And because SIREAD locks escalate to coarser granularity when memory runs low, false positives become more common as read sets grow. That's why the docs recommend keeping serializable transactions short and well indexed, and why `max_pred_locks_per_transaction` exists.

REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation: one snapshot per transaction, ruling out dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms while letting write skew and lost update through. options.text: No. SSI's guarantee covers a set of concurrent serializable transactions, and a Read Committed writer is not tracked, so it can produce anomalies the serializable reader cannot detect.
Yes. SSI tracks read-write dependencies for every transaction regardless of its level, so one serializable participant is enough.
Yes, provided the Read Committed writer touches only rows the serializable transaction has read, since those carry SIREAD locks.
No, but only because Read Committed takes no row locks. Adding `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` to the writer would restore the guarantee.

questions.explanation:
The docs word the promise carefully. If you show that a transaction does the right thing when run alone, "you can have confidence that it will do the right thing in any mix of Serializable transactions, even without any information about what those other transactions might do, or it will not successfully commit." The guarantee covers a mix of *serializable* transactions. Every participant has to opt in, and one transaction can't get it alone.

The mechanism shows why. Serializable transactions record SIREAD locks for what they read, and SSI checks for dangerous structures among those tracked transactions. A Read Committed transaction records nothing and is checked against nothing. SSI can't see it, so it can write straight through a predicate your serializable transaction depends on. No pivot is ever detected, because half the graph was never recorded.

This is one of the most common ways a "we're serializable" claim turns out false in production. It usually breaks at the edges: a migration script, an admin `psql` session, a background worker on a different connection pool, or an ORM whose per-connection isolation setting reset with the pool. If your correctness depends on serializability, set it for the whole database:

```sql
ALTER DATABASE mydb SET default_transaction_isolation = 'serializable';
```

Then make sure every code path has a `40001` retry loop, because every one of them can now fail.

questions.title: How does SSI's approach to serializability differ from classic two-phase locking?

images.alt: Four PostgreSQL isolation level names against what the server actually does. READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted for compatibility and treated as READ COMMITTED. READ COMMITTED, the default, takes a fresh snapshot at the start of every statement rather than of the transaction. REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation: one snapshot per transaction, ruling out dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms while letting write skew and lost update through. SERIALIZABLE adds SSI, which watches for dangerous read/write structures and aborts a transaction instead of taking two-phase locks. Two cards give the SQLSTATE codes to retry on, 40001 serialization_failure and 40P01 deadlock_detected, and a closing note warns that SSI only sees transactions that are themselves SERIALIZABLE, that Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, and that MySQL's InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ.

options.text: 2PL is pessimistic: readers take locks and block writers, so conflicting transactions wait. SSI is optimistic: reads never block anything, and conflicts are resolved by aborting a transaction after the fact.
SSI is pessimistic and 2PL is optimistic. SSI acquires predicate locks upfront while 2PL validates only at commit time.
They are implementation variants of the same algorithm. SSI is 2PL with the lock table stored in shared memory.
2PL guarantees serializability only for read-write transactions, while SSI extends the guarantee to read-only transactions.

questions.explanation:
They take opposite approaches to concurrency control. Both give true serializability, so the difference is in throughput and latency, not correctness.

Two-phase locking has a growing phase that acquires locks and a shrinking phase that releases them. It makes conflicting transactions wait. The main cost is that readers block writers and writers block readers. Long read queries stall writes, tail latency becomes unpredictable, and deadlocks are routine. It was the standard approach for decades, and MySQL/InnoDB still uses it at `SERIALIZABLE`.

SSI keeps MVCC's main promise: readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. Instead, it records reads with SIREAD locks and watches for the pivot pattern. Conflicting transactions run at full speed, and the loser is aborted with `40001`.

This works well under low to moderate contention, where most transactions don't conflict and serializability costs very little. Under heavy contention on a hot row or predicate, SSI turns into a storm of aborts and retries that repeats the same work. There, explicit locking with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` at Read Committed often gets better throughput than `SERIALIZABLE`, because waiting is cheaper than redoing.

questions.title: At `READ COMMITTED`, a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` blocks on a row another transaction is updating. When that transaction commits, what does your query return?

options.text: The new committed version of the row, re-checked against your `WHERE` clause and skipped entirely if it no longer matches, even though that version is newer than your statement's snapshot.
The version of the row as of your statement's snapshot, since a locking read must be consistent with the rest of the query.
Nothing. The row is dropped from the result set whenever a concurrent transaction modified it, to avoid returning inconsistent data.
An error, because a locking read cannot proceed once the row it targeted has changed underneath it.

questions.explanation:
This is documented behavior, and it's the most surprising thing about locking reads at Read Committed. The row you get back can be newer than the rest of your result.

Your `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` finds a matching row in its snapshot, sees that an uncommitted transaction has locked it, and waits. When that transaction commits, PostgreSQL re-reads the latest version and re-checks the `WHERE` clause. If it still matches, you get the new version, locked. If not, the row is skipped and never appears in your results.

The silent skip is the dangerous part. `SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending' LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE` can return zero rows from a table full of pending jobs, because a competing worker grabbed the row it picked and changed its status. `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` makes skipping explicit and is the right tool for queue workers.

So once locking is involved, Read Committed doesn't give you a consistent view even within one statement. Locked rows come from the present, and unlocked rows come from your snapshot. At `REPEATABLE READ`, PostgreSQL raises SQLSTATE `40001` instead. That's a better contract: you get an error you can handle instead of a wrong answer.

questions.title: Why does `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` fail to prevent this double booking?
questions.description:
A booking service checks for a conflicting reservation before inserting one. Two requests for the same room and overlapping times arrive at the same moment, both at `READ COMMITTED`:

```sql
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM bookings
 WHERE room_id = 7
   AND during && tstzrange('2026-09-01 10:00', '2026-09-01 11:00')
 FOR UPDATE;          -- returns 0 rows in both sessions

-- both conclude the slot is free
INSERT INTO bookings (room_id, during) VALUES (7, ...);
COMMIT;
```

images.alt: Three two-transaction timelines with time running downward, all of them committing. Lost update at READ COMMITTED: both sessions read balance 100, one writes 90 and commits, the other writes 80 and commits, leaving 80 and erasing the first change. Write skew at REPEATABLE READ: two doctors each count two colleagues on call, each concludes it is safe to leave, each updates a different row, and both commit with nobody on call. The phantom a row lock cannot hold, at READ COMMITTED: two sessions run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, both get zero rows, both insert a booking for the same room and hour, and both commit.
images.caption: The third timeline: both `SELECT`s locked nothing at all.

options.text: Because there are no rows to lock. The conflicting booking does not exist yet, and a row lock cannot be taken on a row that has not been inserted.
Because `FOR UPDATE` releases its locks as soon as the `SELECT` completes, rather than holding them until commit.
Because `FOR UPDATE` takes a shared lock, so two transactions can hold it on the same rows simultaneously.
Because range overlap predicates on `tstzrange` can't be combined with a locking clause.

questions.explanation:
This is write skew on a phantom. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks the rows the query returns. Here it returns zero rows, so it locks nothing, and nothing stops another transaction from inserting a row that would have matched.

That's the basic limit of row-level locking: you can't lock data that doesn't exist yet. `FOR UPDATE` can't protect any rule of the form "no row exists such that P," whether it's no overlapping booking, no duplicate username, or no second claim on a coupon. What you need to reserve is a gap in the key space, and a row lock can't do that.

Four fixes that work, roughly in order of preference:

1. A real constraint. PostgreSQL's exclusion constraint expresses this rule directly and enforces it at any isolation level:
   ```sql
   ALTER TABLE bookings ADD CONSTRAINT no_overlap
     EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&);
   ```
2. `SERIALIZABLE`. SSI's predicate locks cover the gap, and one transaction gets `40001`.
3. Put the conflict on a real row. Lock the `rooms` row with `FOR UPDATE` first, so both transactions wait on something concrete.
4. A transactional advisory lock keyed on `room_id`. It's the same idea as fix 3, without a row to lock.

MySQL's InnoDB works differently. At `REPEATABLE READ`, its locking reads take next-key locks that cover the row and the gap before it, so it does lock gaps. Different engines have different defaults and different failure modes.

questions.title: What is the practical difference between `pg_advisory_lock(key)` and `pg_advisory_xact_lock(key)`?

options.text: The session-scoped lock is held until you explicitly unlock it or the connection ends, surviving both `COMMIT` and `ROLLBACK`. The transaction-scoped one is released automatically at the end of the transaction and cannot be released early.
The session-scoped lock is advisory only, while the transaction-scoped one is enforced by the storage engine against all statements.
They are identical apart from lock strength. The session-scoped one is exclusive and the transaction-scoped one is shared.
The transaction-scoped lock is released at the end of the current statement, while the session-scoped one lasts for the transaction.

questions.explanation:
Advisory locks are locks with no rows attached. You pick a 64-bit key (or a pair of 32-bit integers), the database gives you mutual exclusion on it, and what the key means is up to you. They're the natural tool when the thing you need to serialize on isn't a row: a gap in a range, a cron job that must run on one instance, or a per-tenant import.

Most advisory-lock incidents come from the scope difference:

```sql
-- transaction-scoped: released at COMMIT or ROLLBACK, always
BEGIN;
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('room:7'));
-- ... check and insert ...
COMMIT;    -- lock gone

-- session-scoped: survives COMMIT, survives ROLLBACK, survives your
-- exception handler. Only pg_advisory_unlock() or disconnect frees it.
SELECT pg_advisory_lock(42);
```

The docs say session-level advisory locks "do not honor transaction semantics: a lock acquired during a transaction that is later rolled back will still be held following the rollback." A session lock leaked by a code path that threw before unlocking doesn't show up in the usual `pg_locks` searches. With a connection pool it's worse than a leak: the connection goes back to the pool still holding the lock, and the next unrelated request that borrows it inherits the lock or deadlocks on it. Unless you need a lock that spans transactions, use `pg_advisory_xact_lock`. Its automatic release is the whole point.

Advisory locks are also purely cooperative. A transaction that doesn't ask for the lock isn't blocked by it, so it only protects you if every code path that touches the resource takes it.

- [PostgreSQL: Advisory Locks](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html#ADVISORY-LOCKS)
- [PostgreSQL: Advisory Lock Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-admin.html#FUNCTIONS-ADVISORY-LOCKS)

questions.title: Which PostgreSQL function takes an exclusive advisory lock that is released automatically when the transaction ends?
questions.description: Give the function name, without arguments.
questions.explanation:
`pg_advisory_xact_lock(key bigint)`, or the two-argument form `pg_advisory_xact_lock(key1 int, key2 int)`, which is handy for namespacing keys by table or tenant.

The naming is systematic, so it's easiest to learn the family as a grid:

| | Session-scoped | Transaction-scoped |
|---|---|---|
| Exclusive, waits | `pg_advisory_lock` | `pg_advisory_xact_lock` |
| Exclusive, no wait | `pg_try_advisory_lock` | `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock` |
| Shared, waits | `pg_advisory_lock_shared` | `pg_advisory_xact_lock_shared` |
| Unlock | `pg_advisory_unlock` | *(not possible)* |

The `try` variants return a `boolean` right away instead of waiting. Use them when only one worker should run a job and the others should skip it instead of queueing:

```sql
SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('nightly-rollup')) AS got_it;
```

There's no `pg_advisory_xact_unlock` on purpose. Only the end of the transaction releases a transaction-scoped lock, which is what makes it impossible to leak.

questions.title: At `READ COMMITTED`, why does a version-column `UPDATE` reliably detect a concurrent change, even though the transaction read the row minutes earlier?
questions.description:
The row carries an integer `version` column, and the write is issued as:

```sql
UPDATE products
   SET price = 19.99, version = version + 1
 WHERE id = 42 AND version = 7;
```

options.text: Because Read Committed re-evaluates the `WHERE` clause against the newest committed row version after unblocking. If another transaction bumped `version`, the predicate no longer matches and the statement reports zero rows updated.
Because the `version` column causes PostgreSQL to promote the statement to `REPEATABLE READ` semantics for that row.
Because `UPDATE` always takes a snapshot at `BEGIN`, so the stale `version` value guarantees a serialization failure.
Because PostgreSQL compares the row's internal `xmin` against the transaction id and aborts on mismatch.

questions.explanation:
Optimistic concurrency control works at Read Committed for the same reason `SET balance = balance - 100` is safe: PostgreSQL re-checks the `WHERE` clause against the current row version. The version column uses that re-check on purpose.

```sql
-- read, long ago (or in a previous HTTP request)
SELECT id, price, version FROM products WHERE id = 42;   -- version = 7

-- write, now
UPDATE products
   SET price = 19.99, version = version + 1
 WHERE id = 42 AND version = 7;
```

Suppose a competing transaction bumps the row to `version = 8` in between. This statement finds `version = 8` (after waiting on the row lock, if that transaction hasn't committed yet), fails the predicate, and updates zero rows. Your application checks the affected-row count (`cmdtuples` in libpq, `rowcount` in most drivers) and reports a conflict.

People often skip that last step, and then a correct algorithm silently loses data, because an `UPDATE` that matches zero rows isn't an error in SQL. Every optimistic write must check the count.

Unlike `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, this holds no lock while the user is thinking. A lock taken when a form opens and released when it's submitted can last minutes and kill concurrency. The version column holds a lock for microseconds and turns a conflict into a retry or a "someone else edited this" message. The downside is that under heavy contention you keep redoing work.

- [Martin Fowler: Optimistic Offline Lock](https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/optimisticOfflineLock.html)

questions.title: Which locking clause should a `SELECT` use so that concurrent plain `UPDATE`s to a row's non-key columns are still allowed, while `DELETE`s and key changes are blocked?

options.text: `FOR KEY SHARE`, the weakest row-level mode, and the one PostgreSQL takes internally for foreign-key checks.
`FOR SHARE`, a shared lock, which by definition permits other readers and writers to proceed.
`FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, which as the name says declines to lock the key, leaving other updaters free.
`FOR UPDATE NOWAIT`, where the `NOWAIT` modifier downgrades the lock so it does not conflict with plain updates.

questions.explanation:
PostgreSQL has four row-level lock modes, from strongest to weakest:

| Mode | Blocks | Typical source |
|---|---|---|
| `FOR UPDATE` | everything, including `FOR KEY SHARE` | explicit; `DELETE` |
| `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` | all but `FOR KEY SHARE` | a plain `UPDATE` not touching key columns |
| `FOR SHARE` | `FOR UPDATE`, `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` | explicit |
| `FOR KEY SHARE` | `FOR UPDATE` only | foreign-key checks |

The modes are named for what the holder plans to do, not for what they allow others to do. `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` means "I'll update this row but not its key." It's stronger than `FOR KEY SHARE`, which means "I need this key to stay as it is."

`FOR KEY SHARE` is the answer because it conflicts only with `FOR UPDATE`. A `DELETE` or a primary-key change is blocked, while a concurrent `UPDATE products SET price = ...`, which only takes `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, goes ahead.

PostgreSQL 9.3 added this split to fix a real production problem. Before it, inserting a child row took a `FOR SHARE` lock on the parent, so bulk inserts of children waited on any update to the parent. With the key-only modes, foreign-key checks stopped blocking unrelated updates. It was a big concurrency win that most users got without ever learning the mode names.

- [PostgreSQL: SELECT, The Locking Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html#SQL-FOR-UPDATE-SHARE)

questions.title: Which of these approaches, used correctly, prevent the double booking?
questions.description: Two concurrent transactions each check that room 7 is free for an overlapping time range, then `INSERT` a booking. Assume `READ COMMITTED` unless the option says otherwise. Select every approach that closes the gap.

images.alt: Three two-transaction timelines with time running downward, all of them committing. Lost update at READ COMMITTED: both sessions read balance 100, one writes 90 and commits, the other writes 80 and commits, leaving 80 and erasing the first change. Write skew at REPEATABLE READ: two doctors each count two colleagues on call, each concludes it is safe to leave, each updates a different row, and both commit with nobody on call. The phantom a row lock cannot hold, at READ COMMITTED: two sessions run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, both get zero rows, both insert a booking for the same room and hour, and both commit.
images.caption: The third timeline is what any correct guard has to prevent.

options.text: An `EXCLUDE USING gist` constraint on `(room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)`.
Running both transactions at `SERIALIZABLE`, with a retry loop for SQLSTATE `40001`.
Taking `pg_advisory_xact_lock(room_id)` at the start of both transactions.
`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the bookings that overlap the requested range.
Adding a `version` column to the `bookings` table and updating with `WHERE version = ?`.

questions.explanation:
The rule is "no row overlaps this range," so for each option, ask whether it can reserve the absence of a row.

The exclusion constraint works. The database enforces the range rule at any isolation level, with no help from application code. That makes it the strongest option, because no code path can skip it.

`SERIALIZABLE` works. SSI's predicate locks record that both transactions read the empty range. The second insert contradicts what the first one read, SSI detects the pivot, and one transaction gets `40001`. This is only correct if you actually retry, and only if both sides run at `SERIALIZABLE`.

The transactional advisory lock works. Locking on `room_id` allows only one writer per room at a time, so check-then-insert becomes atomic in practice. It's cooperative, so it only protects you if every code path takes the lock.

`FOR UPDATE` fails. The overlap query returns zero rows in both sessions, so no locks are taken. You can't lock rows that don't exist.

The version column fails. Optimistic locking protects one existing row from concurrent changes. Here there's no existing row, and the two sessions insert two different new rows, so no version comparison happens. It has the same blind spot as first-committer-wins: it catches update conflicts and misses phantoms.

questions.title: What does Oracle's `SERIALIZABLE` isolation level actually implement?

images.alt: Four PostgreSQL isolation level names against what the server actually does. READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted for compatibility and treated as READ COMMITTED. READ COMMITTED, the default, takes a fresh snapshot at the start of every statement rather than of the transaction. REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation: one snapshot per transaction, ruling out dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms while letting write skew and lost update through. SERIALIZABLE adds SSI, which watches for dangerous read/write structures and aborts a transaction instead of taking two-phase locks. Two cards give the SQLSTATE codes to retry on, 40001 serialization_failure and 40P01 deadlock_detected, and a closing note warns that SSI only sees transactions that are themselves SERIALIZABLE, that Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, and that MySQL's InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ.
images.caption: The same name, one rung lower.

options.text: Snapshot isolation, so it permits write skew despite the name matching the SQL standard's strongest level.
True serializability via strict two-phase locking, the same as MySQL/InnoDB's `SERIALIZABLE`.
Serializable Snapshot Isolation, the same algorithm PostgreSQL adopted in 9.1.
Read Committed with additional predicate locks that eliminate phantom reads only.

questions.explanation:
Oracle's `SERIALIZABLE` is snapshot isolation, and it exposes the SQL standard's biggest weakness. The standard defines isolation levels by the anomalies they must prevent. An implementation that prevents all three named ANSI phenomena (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read) can call itself `SERIALIZABLE` while still allowing write skew, which the 1992 standard never named.

Berenson et al. wrote their 1995 critique to expose this gap. Snapshot isolation blocks all three ANSI phenomena and still isn't serializable, and the standard's definitions can't tell the difference.

This has real consequences. Code that relies on `SERIALIZABLE` to protect an invariant across rows is correct on PostgreSQL 9.1+ and wrong on Oracle, and nothing signals the difference. The on-call doctors and overlapping bookings from earlier questions both break on Oracle at its strongest documented level.

So don't trust level names across engines. Check what each one guarantees. PostgreSQL's `REPEATABLE READ` is snapshot isolation, stronger than the standard requires. Oracle's `SERIALIZABLE` is also snapshot isolation, weaker than its name suggests. MySQL's `REPEATABLE READ` is something else again.

questions.title: Which isolation level does MySQL's InnoDB engine use by default?
questions.description: Answer with the level's name, for example `read committed`.

images.alt: Four PostgreSQL isolation level names against what the server actually does. READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted for compatibility and treated as READ COMMITTED. READ COMMITTED, the default, takes a fresh snapshot at the start of every statement rather than of the transaction. REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation: one snapshot per transaction, ruling out dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms while letting write skew and lost update through. SERIALIZABLE adds SSI, which watches for dangerous read/write structures and aborts a transaction instead of taking two-phase locks. Two cards give the SQLSTATE codes to retry on, 40001 serialization_failure and 40P01 deadlock_detected, and a closing note warns that SSI only sees transactions that are themselves SERIALIZABLE, that Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, and that MySQL's InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ.
images.caption: A different default from PostgreSQL's.

questions.explanation:
InnoDB defaults to `REPEATABLE READ`. So an application moved between MySQL and PostgreSQL silently changes isolation level unless someone sets it explicitly.

InnoDB's implementation behind that name is unusual. At `REPEATABLE READ` it mixes two read mechanisms in one transaction. Plain `SELECT`s (consistent non-locking reads) read from the transaction's MVCC snapshot, taken at the first read. Locking reads (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, `SELECT ... LOCK IN SHARE MODE`, and the row matching inside `UPDATE` and `DELETE`) read the latest committed version instead.

So in one transaction you can `SELECT` a row and see one value, then `UPDATE` that row based on a newer value. Locking reads also take next-key locks on the row and the gap before it. That's why InnoDB blocks phantom inserts for locking reads, while PostgreSQL's snapshot approach just never shows them.

Amazon RDS, Aurora, and several MySQL-compatible forks ship or recommend `READ-COMMITTED` instead, partly because next-key gap locking at `REPEATABLE READ` often causes contention and deadlocks. Jepsen's analysis of MySQL 8.0.34 found its `REPEATABLE READ` allowing anomalies the name doesn't suggest. That's one more reason to check what a level does instead of trusting its name.

questions.title: In the Adya-style anomaly taxonomy that Jepsen's Elle checker uses, what does G1a describe?

options.text: An aborted read: a transaction read a value written by another transaction that ultimately aborted.
An intermediate read: a transaction read a value that was later overwritten within the same writing transaction before it committed.
A write cycle: a set of transactions whose writes form a cycle in the version order.
An anti-dependency cycle: a cycle containing at least one read-write dependency edge.

questions.explanation:
Adya's thesis replaced the SQL standard's informal phenomena with a formal graph model. Jepsen's Elle checker uses it because it doesn't depend on any implementation: you infer the dependency graph from observed histories and look for cycles.

The vocabulary:

- G0, dirty write: a cycle made only of write-write dependencies.
- G1a, aborted read: a transaction read a value written by a transaction that later aborted.
- G1b, intermediate read: a transaction read a value that its writer overwrote before committing, so it was never a final state.
- G1c, circular information flow: a cycle of write-write and write-read dependencies.
- G2-item: a cycle that includes a read-write anti-dependency on a specific item.
- G2: the general anti-dependency cycle. Write skew is one example.

Each isolation level is then defined by which of these it forbids. Read Committed forbids G0 and G1. Repeatable Read also forbids G2-item. Snapshot isolation forbids G0, G1, and a specific structural variant. Serializability forbids all cycles.

The advantage is that you can check it. Elle can look at a real database's history and say "this system exhibits G2-item," a testable claim about behavior instead of a reading of the manual. That's how Jepsen keeps finding shipped isolation levels that don't match their docs.

questions.title: Every transaction now runs at `SERIALIZABLE` with a retry loop. Which kind of bug does this still leave untouched?

options.text: Side effects outside the database, such as sending an email, calling a payment API, or writing a cache. A retry runs them again, and an abort can't undo them.
Write skew between two transactions that read and write disjoint rows, which SSI can't detect.
Lost updates in read-modify-write code, which require an explicit version column at every isolation level.
Phantom reads, since predicate locking covers only rows that already exist.

questions.explanation:
Serializability is a guarantee about the database's state, and it ends at the database's boundary. Anything your transaction does to the outside world isn't covered.

The retry loop that `SERIALIZABLE` requires makes this easy to see:

```python
for attempt in range(5):
    try:
        with conn.transaction():
            order = create_order(...)
            charge_card(order)        # external API call
            send_confirmation(order)  # external API call
        break
    except SerializationFailure:
        continue                      # the DB rolls back; Stripe does not
```

If the transaction aborts with `40001` after `charge_card` succeeds, the database rolls back cleanly, but the customer has still been charged. Retry, and you may charge them twice. Serializability did its job, and the money is still wrong.

The usual fix is to keep side effects out of the transaction. Inside the transaction, commit a row that records the intent. Afterwards, a separate worker reads that row and makes the external call, using an idempotency key the remote service deduplicates on. Stripe's idempotency keys exist for exactly this. The pattern is called the transactional outbox.

The other three options are all things serializability does fix, which is what makes them tempting.
